Page 1 
 
Cultivation of Pleurotus ostreatus in Martian Regolith Simulant 
(MGS-1) for Dual-Purpose Food and Construction Applications 
 
Plant The Moon Challenges: Plant Mars | Spring 2026 | Undergraduate & Professional Division 
 
Team Members from left to right: 
Addison Necciai, Reese Laushot, Helen Navach, David Kimberly, Carolyn Conrad 
 
Team Marshroom | Team #25205 
University of Central Florida | Orlando, FL

Page 2 
 
Abstract 
Establishing sustainable food production and construction material systems on Mars represents 
one of the most critical challenges for long-duration space exploration. This study investigated the 
feasibility of cultivating Pleurotus ostreatus (oyster mushrooms) across nine substrate formulations 
containing varying ratios of Martian regolith simulant (MGS-1), powdered straw or sawdust, 
wheat bran, and gypsum, with the dual goal of producing edible fruiting bodies and structural 
mycelium-based composites (myco-bricks). Substrates were inoculated with P. ostreatus spawn 
cultivated on Uncle Ben's rice bags and monitored over an 8-week period for colonization 
progression, fruiting body formation, and brick consolidation. Environmental conditions were 
tracked using Inkbird hygrometers and ranged from 18.0–22.5°C with relative humidity between 
66–96%. Mycelial colonization was observed in several batches, particularly those with higher 
organic content, but growth stalled within 2–3 weeks in all substrates. No fruiting bodies or 
structurally consolidated bricks were produced. The control substrate (90% MGS-1) showed the 
weakest colonization. Contamination from a competing mold species, inconsistent watering, lack 
of HEPA filtration, and uncontrolled airflow in the atrium incubation environment are identified 
as the primary constraints on fungal development. These findings contribute to the growing body 
of literature on fungal cultivation in regolith-based systems and highlight the critical importance 
of environmental control for mycelium-based ISRU applications on Mars.

Page 3 
 
Introduction & Theory 
Introduction 
Long-duration space missions face strict mass, volume, and resource constraints, making in-situ 
resource utilization (ISRU) essential for sustainable extraterrestrial living. Every kilogram 
launched into space increases mission cost and complexity, and every additional item introduces 
new variables and potential points of failure. For future Martian habitats, systems that serve 
multiple functions—such as producing food while also generating construction materials—are 
especially valuable. 
Fungi, particularly oyster mushrooms (Pleurotus ostreatus), present a promising avenue for 
multifunctional ISRU systems. Oyster mushrooms can convert low-value organic substrates into 
edible fruiting bodies while simultaneously producing mycelium, a dense fibrous network capable 
of forming lightweight, insulating, and biodegradable structural materials (Islam et al., 2017). 
Mycelium-based composites have been studied for their mechanical strength, adaptability, and 
potential as sustainable building materials. 
Fresh food also plays a critical psychological and nutritional role in isolated environments. Studies 
show that access to fresh produce improves well-being and morale during spaceflight and military 
missions (Trovato et al., 2025). Mushrooms are particularly suitable for space agriculture due to 
their compact growth requirements, rapid life cycle, and ability to grow on recycled substrates 
(Cotter, 2014). 
This experiment explores whether P. ostreatus can be cultivated in Martian regolith simulant 
(MGS-1) supplemented with organic materials to produce both edible mushrooms and structural 
mycelium bricks. Understanding fungal growth behavior in regolith-based substrates is a key step 
toward developing integrated food-and-material systems for future Martian settlements. Notably, 
a parallel study by Chavez et al. (2025) in the same Plant the Moon Challenge season also explored 
P. ostreatus in MGS-1, finding that sealed, high-humidity environments facilitated more robust 
mycelial colonization than open pot-based substrates—a finding that aligns closely with the 
constraints encountered in our own study.

Page 4 
 
Theory: The key consideration in this experimental design was the composition of the soil, which 
once colonized could hypothetically be concretized. Given previous experimental success with 
growing Pleurotus ostreatus to flush in Exo-Regolith simulant, by past Plant the Moon teams, the 
procedure was designed specifically to experiment with creating growth medium recipe conducive 
to creating a structurally sound myco-concrete. Definitionally, some concrete is the mixture of a 
cementing medium with a fine aggregate, (Neville, 2010) usually silicates which also comprises 
46% of MGS-1 Global Version. (Long-Fox, 2023) Myco-concrete, lacking a traditional cementing 
medium, instead binds the aggregate matrix in a dense mycelium network. Through the 
colonization of lignocellulosic aggregate components, in this case saw dust or straw dust, Pleurotus 
ostreatus will in theory extend a network of hyphae between the aggregates, compacting the 
smaller substrate particulates. (Zhang, 2025) Saw dust and straw dust, both being common 
lignocellulosic substrates for P. ostreatus cultivation, exist as independent variable 
groupings. These groupings test efficiency in growth rate, as well as composite strength in the 
matrix, as each has a unique particulate size, mass, and density, which could affect the structural

maturation. Once Pleurotus ostreatus fully colonizes its aggregate matrix, the fungus begins the 
production of its fruiting bodies, which results ultimately in considerable fungal die back. Such 
an event is not preferable and as such fruiting must be prevented, by way of heating and trying the 
newly formed ‘composite myco-cement’ mixture into a solid non-living structure. Fungal concrete 
using P. ostreatus is already common in engineering experimentation as a more sustainable 
alternative to semi-permanent building materials, however changing the aggregate base from a 
terrestrial silicate mixture to one of Martian origin is still a new and widely unexplored 
venture. Consideration should be made regarding the biological interactions between components 
found in Martian regolith that P. ostreatus would find unfamiliar in its usual life cycle, as they may 
lead to variation in growth compared to terrestrial myco-concrete recipes. 
 
The importance in testing both the growth of these fungi into edible fruit as well as into a structural 
composite, returns to the core principle of ISRU, which is limiting payload weight on rockets. In 
this case, should the fungus be capable of both fruiting and composing a structure it may then be 
possible to reuse once or twice spent mycelium post fruiting as the basis for growing concrete.

Page 5 
 
Hypothesis 
Research Question: Can Pleurotus ostreatus be successfully cultivated in substrate formulations 
containing Martian regolith simulant (MGS-1) and lignocellulosic organic matter to produce both 
edible fruiting bodies and structurally consolidated mycelium-based composites (myco-bricks) 
suitable for in-situ resource utilization (ISRU) on Mars? 
 
Hypothesis: When cultivated in optimized substrates composed of powdered straw or sawdust, 
nutritional supplements, and Martian regolith simulant, Pleurotus ostreatus will exhibit enhanced 
mycelial development and produce fruiting bodies suitable for consumption. The resulting 
mycelium will bind the substrate into a solid composite capable of functioning as ISRU myco-
concrete. 
 
The scientific basis for this hypothesis rests on four key areas of research: 
 
1. Fungal Growth Requirements: Oyster mushrooms require a carbon-rich substrate (straw, 
sawdust), nitrogen supplementation (wheat bran), minerals such as calcium sulfate 
(gypsum), and adequate moisture and oxygen. Previous studies show that substrate 
composition significantly affects colonization speed and yield (Z.A.S. et al., 2004; 
Moonmoon et al., 2010). 
2. Role of Gypsum and Supplements: Gypsum has been shown to improve fungal growth and 
fruiting by enhancing substrate structure and mineral availability (Li et al., 2022). 
3. Mycelium as a Structural Material: Mycelium forms a dense, interwoven network of 
hyphae that can bind particulate materials into lightweight composites with measurable 
compressive strength (Islam et al., 2017). When grown in molds, this network can create 
"myco-bricks" suitable for construction. 
4. Relevance to Martian ISRU: Using Martian regolith as a bulk substrate reduces the need 
to transport building materials from Earth. If fungi can grow in regolith-based mixtures, 
they could simultaneously support food production, waste recycling, and construction of 
habitat components.

Page 6 
 
Experimental Variables 
 
Independent Variables 
Independent variables are the factors deliberately manipulated across experimental batches to evaluate their 
effect on fungal growth and composite formation. 
1. Type of lignocellulosic substrate: Powdered strawdust versus fine sawdust was used as the 
primary carbon source across the eight experimental batches (Batches 1–4 used strawdust; Batches 
5–8 used sawdust). These two materials differ in particulate size, density, and lignocellulosic 
composition, potentially affecting both colonization rate and myco-brick structural integrity. 
2. Proportion of MGS-1 Martian regolith simulant: The percentage of MGS-1 in each batch was 
varied across four levels: 50%, 55%, 60%, and 65% (with the balance made up by the 
lignocellulosic source). The control batch contained 90% MGS-1 with no lignocellulosic 
component. This gradient was designed to determine the maximum regolith concentration at which 
P. ostreatus can still colonize and potentially form a structural composite. 
 
Dependent Variables 
Dependent variables are the measurable outcomes observed in response to the manipulated independent 
variables. 
1. Mycelial colonization rate and extent: The speed and completeness of white mycelial thread 
growth through each substrate batch, assessed qualitatively (none, light, moderate, heavy) through 
weekly visual inspection and photographic documentation. 
2. Fruiting body formation: The presence, number, and size of primordia and mature Pleurotus 
ostreatus fruiting bodies produced in the fruiting bag format across all nine substrate batches. 
3. Myco-brick structural consolidation: The degree to which the inoculated substrate in brick molds 
(10 × 1.25 × 1.25 inches) consolidated into a self-supporting solid composite, assessed by handling 
and visual inspection at the end of the 8-week period. 
 
Controlled Variables 
Controlled variables are factors held constant across all batches to ensure that observed differences in 
outcomes are attributable to the independent variables rather than extraneous influences.

Page 7 
 
1. Fungal species: Pleurotus ostreatus (oyster mushroom) was used as the sole inoculum species 
across all nine batches, ensuring that any differences in colonization are due to substrate 
composition rather than species variation. 
2. Spawn source and inoculation method: All nine batches were inoculated from the same four 
Uncle Ben’s ready-to-eat rice bag spawns, ensuring a consistent and genetically identical inoculum 
was distributed evenly across all substrates. 
3. Supplemental components (wheat bran and gypsum): All experimental batches (excluding the 
control) contained a fixed 5% wheat bran (nitrogen supplement) and 5% food-grade gypsum 
(calcium sulfate), ensuring that nutritional supplementation was equivalent across all batches. 
4. Incubation environment and duration: All batches were incubated in the same engineering 
atrium location using two identical covered containers monitored with Inkbird digital 
hygrometer/thermometers. The experimental period was fixed at 8 weeks for all batches, with 
environmental monitoring conducted from March 9–29, 2025. 
5. Substrate format (brick molds and fruiting bags): Each of the nine substrate batches was 
simultaneously prepared in two formats: a 10 × 1.25 × 1.25-inch brick mold for structural composite 
assessment and a fruiting bag in a 3D-printed 3 × 3 × 3-inch box for mushroom production 
assessment. This dual format was kept consistent across all batches. 
6. MGS-1 source and preparation: All batches used Martian regolith simulant sourced from the 
same Plant the Moon Challenge kit supply to ensure consistent mineral composition (MGS-1 
Global Version) across the experiment. 
 
Measurement Methods 
 
Experimental Design Overview 
The experiment tested nine substrate formulations containing varying ratios of Martian regolith simulant 
(MGS-1), gypsum, wheat bran, and either powdered straw or sawdust. Each substrate was inoculated with 
P. ostreatus mycelium and monitored for colonization, fruiting, and structural formation over an 8-week 
period (March 9 – March 29, 2025 for environmental monitoring; inoculation began approximately 6 weeks 
prior).

Spawn Preparation 
Initial Attempt (Discarded): Ten wheat-bran bags were inoculated with P. ostreatus spores but developed 
mold contamination and were entirely discarded prior to substrate inoculation. 
Successful Spawn: Four Uncle Ben's ready rice bags were subsequently inoculated with P. ostreatus spores 
and successfully colonized. These colonized rice bags served as the primary inoculation source for all nine 
substrate batches.

Page 9 
 
Inoculation Procedure 
Rice spawns were broken apart and mixed evenly into each substrate batch. Substrates were then placed 
into two formats: nine brick molds (10 × 1.25 × 1.25 inches) intended for myco-brick formation, and nine 
fruiting bags inserted in a 3 x 3 x 3 inches 3D printed boxes intended for mushroom production. All 
samples were distributed across two incubation containers and placed in an atrium environment. 
 
Environmental Conditions and Monitoring 
Environmental conditions were monitored using two Inkbird digital hygrometer/thermometers, one placed 
in each incubation container. Temperature and relative humidity readings were recorded approximately 
every 1–2 days from March 9 to March 29, 2025. Figures 2a and 2b below summarize the recorded 
environmental data: 
 
Figure 2a. Temperature recorded in both incubation containers (March 9–29, 2025). Solid lines = daily maximum; 
dashed lines = daily minimum. Shaded band = optimal growth range (18–24°C). Optimal conditions for P. ostreatus 
mycelial growth are generally 18–24°C and 80–95% relative humidity (Cotter, 2014).

Page 10 
 
 
Figure 2b. Relative humidity in both incubation containers (March 9–29, 2025). Solid lines = daily high; dashed 
lines = daily low. Green shaded band = optimal RH range for P. ostreatus colonization (80–95%, Cotter, 2014). 
 
Constraints on environmental control were significant. The experiment was conducted in an engineering 
atrium with uncontrolled airflow. A still-air box was introduced partway through the experiment to reduce 
contamination risk but did not fully eliminate it. Temperature and humidity fluctuated considerably, 
particularly in Container 2 during Week 4 where minimums dropped to 15°C and 67% RH—conditions 
below the threshold for optimal mycelial activity. Watering was inconsistent throughout the experiment. No 
HEPA filtration or sterile laboratory equipment was available. 
 
Measurement Techniques 
Due to the absence of fruiting bodies and incomplete colonization, quantitative yield data could not be 
collected. The following qualitative and observational methods were employed: 
• 
Qualitative colonization scoring via visual inspection (none, light, moderate, heavy) 
• 
Photographic documentation of substrate, hygrometer readings, and environmental setup 
• 
Daily and weekly observation logs of mycelial progression and contamination 
• 
Structural integrity assessment of brick molds for early consolidation

Page 11 
 
Analysis & Results 
 
Colonization Outcomes 
Mycelial colonization was observed in several batches during the first 1–2 weeks of incubation, with the 
most visible growth appearing in substrates containing higher proportions of organic material (Batches 1 
and 5, with 40% straw/sawdust respectively). However, growth stalled or reversed in all batches within 2–
3 weeks. No primordia or fruiting bodies were observed in any substrate at any point during the 8-week 
experiment. No substrate achieved the degree of full colonization required for myco-brick consolidation4

Figure 1. Spawn colonization increased slowly during the first two weeks after inoculation. Rapid expansion began

Contamination 
The first round of spawn preparation (wheat-bran bags) was lost entirely to mold contamination before any 
substrate inoculation occurred. Subsequent batches inoculated with the rice-bag spawn showed no 
macroscopically visible mold; however, the stalling and dieback of mycelium in all batches suggests the 
likely presence of microbial competition at a level not detectable by visual inspection alone. 
 
Environmental Data Summary 
Temperature across both containers remained within the acceptable range for P. ostreatus growth (18–24°C) 
for most of the experiment. However, relative humidity was highly inconsistent. Container 2 showed a 
marked decline in humidity during Week 4, reaching minimums of 15°C and 67% RH, which falls below 
the threshold for sustained mycelial activity. Container 1 maintained more consistent humidity (78–96%) 
but experienced its own periods of lower readings (67–75% in mid-experiment). The ideal humidity for P. 
ostreatus colonization is 80–95% (Cotter, 2014), which was achieved only intermittently in both containers.

Page 13 
 
Overall Result 
The primary hypothesis—that P. ostreatus cultivated in MGS-1-based substrates supplemented with organic 
materials would produce fruiting bodies and consolidate into myco-bricks—could not be confirmed or 
rejected due to incomplete colonization and absence of fruiting. The experiment yielded important negative 
data regarding the constraints of non-sterile, non-climate-controlled environments on fungal cultivation in 
regolith-based substrates. 
Discussion & Conclusions 
The results of this study, while not achieving the desired outcome of fruiting body or myco-brick 
production, provide meaningful insights into the challenges of cultivating P. ostreatus in Martian regolith 
simulant under resource-limited conditions. The experiment serves as an important exploratory data point 
in a field where negative results are underreported but equally valuable. 
 
The most significant limiting factor was the lack of environmental control. Oyster mushroom cultivation is 
highly sensitive to humidity fluctuations and airborne contamination. In professional mycology settings, 
HEPA-filtered clean rooms and humidity-controlled fruiting chambers are standard practice. Our atrium-
based setup, while innovative in its use of two separate incubation containers and hygrometer monitoring, 
could not replicate these conditions. The recorded humidity data clearly shows periods where both 
containers fell below the 80% threshold critical for sustained mycelial growth—particularly Container 2 
during the final week, where minimums reached 67% RH and 15°C. 
 
The initial contamination of the wheat-bran spawn also set the experiment back significantly. The successful 
pivot to Uncle Ben's rice bags—a well-documented low-tech spawn cultivation method in the hobby 
mycology community—demonstrated adaptability, but the delay likely reduced the window for full 
substrate colonization within the 8-week period. 
 
Inconsistent watering represents another critical variable. Fungal mycelium requires consistent substrate 
moisture (field capacity ~60–70%) to colonize effectively. Without automated or precision watering, 
moisture levels almost certainly fluctuated in ways not captured by surface hygrometer readings, 
contributing to mycelial dieback in later weeks.

Page 14 
 
 
These findings align closely with the parallel study by Chavez et al. (2025), who also cultivated P. ostreatus 
in MGS-1 during the same Plant the Moon Challenge season. That team similarly encountered mold 
contamination that outcompeted their target fungi, and found that only their sealed bag environment—
where humidity was maintained by the mycelium's own respiration—produced robust colonization. Their 
open pot-based specimens, analogous to our setup, showed slower and more inconsistent progression. This 
convergence of results across two independent studies using similar organisms and substrates strongly 
suggests that environmental sealing and humidity control are non-negotiable prerequisites for successful 
fungal ISRU systems. 
 
The control batch (90% MGS-1, no organic carbon source) performed worst, as expected. MGS-1 alone 
provides no bioavailable carbon or nitrogen for fungal metabolism, confirming that organic 
supplementation is essential—a finding consistent with the broader Plant the Moon Challenge literature 
(Chavez et al., 2025; Duri et al., 2020). 
 
Future iterations of this experiment should prioritize: (1) a sealed, humidity-controlled fruiting chamber 
maintaining 85–95% RH consistently; (2) HEPA filtration or at minimum a laminar flow hood for all 
inoculation procedures; (3) automated or precision watering protocols; (4) extended colonization periods 
of 10–12 weeks before fruiting induction; and (5) the inclusion of P. ostreatus spawn specifically cultivated 
on straw rather than rice, as straw more closely resembles the carbon structure of the organic substrates 
used. Additionally, future studies should explore the potential of fully sealed bag cultures within the 
substrate molds themselves, combining the sealed humidity advantage observed by Chavez et al. (2025) 
with the brick-formation goal of our own study. 
 
Despite the absence of fruiting bodies or myco-bricks, this experiment makes a genuine contribution to the 
literature on fungal ISRU for Mars. It documents a set of environmental conditions under which P. ostreatus 
cannot be reliably cultivated in MGS-1-based substrates, narrows the design space for future experiments, 
and provides the first multi-batch regolith ratio comparison (50–65% MGS-1 vs. organic content) in a non-
sterile setting. As one of very few teams in the Plant the Moon Challenge to pursue a dual food-and-material 
system through a single organism.

Appendix B: Substrate Preparation Notes 
All substrate components were weighed and mixed by hand. Mixing was performed thoroughly to ensure 
even distribution of nutrients. MGS-1 Martian regolith simulant was provided by the Plant the Moon 
Challenge kit. Wheat bran (nitrogen supplement) and food-grade gypsum (calcium sulfate) were sourced 
commercially. Powdered straw and fine sawdust were sourced locally and ground to a fine consistency 
before mixing. Substrate batches were prepared simultaneously and inoculated within 24 hours of 
preparation.

Page 16 
 
Appendix C: Spawn Preparation Notes 
First spawn attempt: ten wheat-bran bags were inoculated with P. ostreatus spores under non-sterile 
conditions using a still-air box. All ten bags developed green/black mold contamination within seven days 
and were discarded. 
 
Second spawn attempt: four Uncle Ben's ready-to-eat rice bags were inoculated with P. ostreatus spores. 
Rice bags were sanitized externally with isopropyl alcohol prior to inoculation. All four bags showed 
successful white mycelial colonization within 10–14 days and were used as the inoculation source for all 
nine substrate batches.
